import seaborn as sns

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
plt.style.use("ggplot")
plt.rcParams.update({"figure.figsize": (8, 5), "figure.dpi": 100, "savefig.dpi": 300,

import matplotlib as mpl

mpl.rcParams['axes.prop_cycle'] = cycler(color=[slate, blue, turquoise, orange, red, green, purple, red_pink])

import torch
torch.manual_seed(1)
from statsmodels.tsa.seasonal import STL
from statsforecast import StatsForecast
from statsforecast.models import AutoETS, Naive, SeasonalNaive
from great_tables import GT, loc, style as gt_style
from matplotlib.colors import LinearSegmentedColormap, to_hex

shade = LinearSegmentedColormap.from_list("shade", ["#bfe0b0", "#ffffff", "#f5b8cb"])


def scoreboard(table, rules=None, decimals=2, size="0.8em"):
    """A results table: green is better, pink is worse, the best in bold."""
    df = table.to_frame() if isinstance(table, pd.Series) else table.copy()
    df.index = [str(i) for i in df.index]
    df.columns = [str(c) for c in df.columns]
    rules = rules or {c: "lower" for c in df.columns}
    gt = (GT(df.reset_index(names="row"), rowname_col="row")
          .fmt_number(columns=list(df.select_dtypes("number").columns), decimals=decimals)
          .sub_missing(missing_text="")
          .tab_options(table_font_size=size, data_row_padding="3px"))
    for c, rule in rules.items():
        values = df[c].astype(float)
        bad = values if rule == "lower" else -values if rule == "higher" else (values - rule).abs()
        lo, hi = np.nanmin(bad), np.nanmax(bad)
        for i, b in enumerate(bad):
            if np.isnan(b):
                continue
            fill = to_hex(shade((b - lo) / (hi - lo) if hi > lo else 0.0))
            look = [gt_style.fill(color=fill)] + ([gt_style.text(weight="bold")] if b == np.nanmin(bad) else [])
            gt = gt.tab_style(style=look, locations=loc.body(columns=c, rows=[i]))
    return gt


def box(ax, x, y, w, h, text, colour, size=12):
    ax.add_patch(FancyBboxPatch((x, y), w, h, boxstyle="round,pad=0.02", facecolor="white",
                                edgecolor=colour, linewidth=2))
    ax.text(x + w / 2, y + h / 2, text, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=size)


views = pd.read_csv("../data/pageviews.csv", parse_dates=["ds"])
series = {name: g.set_index("ds")["y"] for name, g in views.groupby("unique_id")}
thousands = mpl.ticker.FuncFormatter(lambda v, _: f"{v / 1000:,.0f}k")

# Why forecast at all

## Every plan is a forecast {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
Whether or not anyone calls it that, a digital business forecasts every week:

| Decision | The forecast behind it |
|---|---|
| Next month's ad budget | installs, CPI, conversion |
| Servers, support shifts | traffic, tickets by hour |
| Revenue plan for the board | subscriptions, renewals, churn |
| When a campaign pays back | the cohort's revenue curve |
| An alert on a dashboard | "what is normal today?" |
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
A useful forecast has four parts:

1. **A number** — the most likely value.
2. **A range** — how wrong it can reasonably be.
3. **A horizon** — how far ahead it is honest.
4. **A decision** it feeds. A forecast nobody acts on is a chart.

[Today: how to get all four — and whether the new AI models get them better than the old tools.]{.hi}
:::
::::

## What is new in 2026 {.smaller}

You already use **foundation models** for text: one model, trained on most of the internet, answers
questions about documents it has never seen.

Since 2023–24 the same idea exists for **time series**: models trained on **hundreds of billions** of data
points — web traffic, energy, retail, weather — that forecast **your** metric with **no training at
all**. Amazon, Google, Salesforce and Nixtla release them; most are free.

Three questions for today:

- **Do they work** on the kind of numbers you look at — product attention, sales, traffic?
- **Where do they fail**, and how do you notice before the board does?
- **Can't I just paste the numbers into ChatGPT or Claude?** We will measure it.

::: {.callout-note}
## Our data today

Daily **Wikipedia page views** of real products and events — ChatGPT, Duolingo, Spotify, Netflix, Tinder,
Strava, TikTok, Notion, Threads, Black Friday. A public, honest proxy for **attention** to a product, with
the same habits as your dashboards: weekly rhythms, seasons, campaigns, launches, decline.
:::

# The basics: reading a time series

## Four things every series is made of {.smaller}

```{python}
#| label: anatomy
#| fig-align: center
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(13, 5.4))
cases = [("Tinder", "2019-01-01", "Trend: slow decline over years", slate),
         ("ChatGPT", "2026-07-01", "Weekly season: weekdays vs weekends", blue),
         ("Black Friday", "2019-01-01", "Yearly event: the same week every year", turquoise),
         ("Duolingo", "2024-09-01", "Shock: a one-off campaign", red_pink)]
for ax, (name, start, title, colour) in zip(axes.ravel(), cases):
    s = series[name][start:]
    ax.plot(s.index, s.values, color=colour, linewidth=0.9)
    ax.set_title(f"{name} — {title}", fontsize=11)
    ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(thousands)
plt.show()
```

**Trend**, **season**, **events**, **noise** — every method, classical or AI, separates these four and
extends the first three.

## Taking a series apart {.smaller}

```{python}
#| label: stl
#| fig-align: center
chatgpt = series["ChatGPT"]["2025-01-01":]
parts = STL(np.log(chatgpt), period=7, robust=True).fit()
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(13, 3.2))
axes[0].plot(chatgpt.index, np.exp(parts.trend), color=blue)
axes[0].set_title("Trend (weekly rhythm removed)")
axes[0].yaxis.set_major_formatter(thousands)
week = pd.Series(np.exp(parts.seasonal.values), index=chatgpt.index).groupby(chatgpt.index.dayofweek).mean()
axes[1].bar(["Mon", "Tue", "Wed", "Thu", "Fri", "Sat", "Sun"], week.values - 1, color=turquoise)
axes[1].set_title("Weekly season: % above an average day")
axes[1].yaxis.set_major_formatter(mpl.ticker.PercentFormatter(1.0))
axes[2].plot(chatgpt.index, np.exp(parts.resid) - 1, color="grey", linewidth=0.6)
axes[2].set_title("What is left: noise and events")
axes[2].yaxis.set_major_formatter(mpl.ticker.PercentFormatter(1.0))
plt.show()
```

- **Weekly season:** Tuesday and Wednesday are about **16%** above an average day, Saturday about **22%**
  below — the rhythm of work and study. Any forecast that misses it is wrong every weekend.
- **Trend:** after the weekly rhythm is removed, what remains moves slowly — that is what a forecast
  extends.
- **What is left** is mostly small noise, with a few huge days: events no history explains.

## The first forecasts to try {.smaller}

Before any model, three rules anyone can compute in a spreadsheet:

```{python}
#| label: baselines
#| fig-align: center
s = series["ChatGPT"]["2026-08-01":"2026-10-24"]
cut = pd.Timestamp("2026-09-26")
hist, future = s[:cut], s[cut + pd.Timedelta(days=1):]
h = len(future)
rules = {"naive: same as yesterday": np.repeat(hist.iloc[-1], h),
         "seasonal naive: same day last week": hist.iloc[-7:].to_numpy()[np.arange(h) % 7],
         "average of the last 4 weeks": np.repeat(hist.iloc[-28:].mean(), h)}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 3.4))
ax.plot(s.index, s.values, color=slate, linewidth=1, label="actual")
for (name, f), colour in zip(rules.items(), [orange, red_pink, blue]):
    ax.plot(future.index, f, color=colour, linewidth=1.8, label=name)
ax.axvline(cut, color="grey", linewidth=0.8)
ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(thousands)
ax.legend(loc="lower left", fontsize=8, ncol=3)
ax.set_title("ChatGPT page views: four weeks ahead from 26 September 2026")
plt.show()
print({name: f"MAE {np.mean(np.abs(future.values - f)) / 1000:.1f}k" for name, f in rules.items()})
```

These are the **benchmarks**. A model — any model, however clever — earns its place only by beating
them on data it has not seen. Surprisingly often, it does not.

## Judging a forecast honestly: backtesting {.smaller}

```{python}
#| label: backtest
#| fig-align: center
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 2.0))
for k in range(4):
    y = 3 - k
    ax.add_patch(plt.Rectangle((0, y), 6 + k, 0.6, color=blue, alpha=0.6))
    ax.add_patch(plt.Rectangle((6 + k, y), 1, 0.6, color=red_pink, alpha=0.8))
    ax.text(-0.2, y + 0.3, f"window {k + 1}", ha="right", va="center", fontsize=13)
ax.text(3, 4.0, "history the model may use", color=blue, ha="center", fontsize=13)
ax.text(10, 4.0, "the period to forecast", color=red_pink, ha="center", fontsize=13)
ax.set_xlim(-2, 12)
ax.set_ylim(-0.2, 4.4)
ax.axis("off")
plt.show()
```

- Cut the history at a past date, forecast the next weeks, **compare with what actually happened**.
  Move the cut forward and repeat: one window is luck, six windows are evidence.
- **Never** judge a model on the data it was fitted to, and never shuffle days at random — the future
  must stay in the future.
- Score with an error you can explain: **MAE** (average miss, in views), **MAPE** (average miss, in %).

::: {.callout-note}
## For analysts

MAPE explodes near zero and rewards under-forecasting; compare models with a **scaled** error instead.
We use **MASE**: the model's MAE divided by the MAE of "same day last week" in the past. Below 1 —
better than that rule.
:::

## A range, not a number {.smaller}

```{python}
#| label: quantiles
#| fig-align: center
from chronos import BaseChronosPipeline

chronos2 = BaseChronosPipeline.from_pretrained("amazon/chronos-2", device_map="cpu")
context = torch.tensor(hist.values, dtype=torch.float32)
q, _ = chronos2.predict_quantiles([torch.tensor(series["ChatGPT"][:cut].values, dtype=torch.float32)],
                                  prediction_length=h, quantile_levels=[0.1, 0.5, 0.9])
q = np.asarray(q[0]).reshape(h, 3)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 3.3))
ax.plot(s.index, s.values, color=slate, linewidth=1, label="actual")
ax.fill_between(future.index, q[:, 0], q[:, 2], color=red_pink, alpha=0.2, label="P10–P90")
ax.plot(future.index, q[:, 1], color=red_pink, linewidth=2, label="P50 (median)")
ax.axvline(cut, color="grey", linewidth=0.8)
ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(thousands)
ax.legend(loc="lower left", fontsize=8)
plt.show()
inside = np.mean((future.values >= q[:, 0]) & (future.values <= q[:, 2]))
print(f"Days inside the P10–P90 band: {inside:.0%} (a calibrated band holds about 80%)")
```

- **P50**: half the days will be above, half below. **P10 / P90**: a bad case and a good case.
- Budget to P50, keep the cash for P90, check that P10 does not break anything.
- The band is only worth something if it is **calibrated**: count how often reality falls inside.

## The classical toolbox, in one slide {.smaller}

| Method | Idea | Good at | Weak at |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Seasonal naive** | repeat last week / last year | strong seasons | everything else |
| **Exponential smoothing (ETS)** | recent past weighs more | level, trend, one season | events, several seasons |
| **ARIMA** | regression on its own past | short-term dynamics | long horizons, regime changes |
| **Prophet** | trend + seasons + holidays | readable, quick | no memory of yesterday |
| **Gradient boosting** (LightGBM) | features → number, across many series | many similar series | needs feature work |

: {tbl-colwidths="[20,30,25,25]"}

All of them are **fitted to your series**: someone chooses the model, its settings, its features, and
refits it as data arrive. That is the work a foundation model promises to remove.

# Foundation models for time series

## The same idea as your chat assistant {.smaller}

```{python}
#| label: fm-idea
#| fig-align: center
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 2.7))
box(ax, 0.0, 0.35, 2.6, 0.5, "billions of points\nfrom thousands of domains", slate)
box(ax, 3.3, 0.35, 2.0, 0.5, "pretraining\n(once, on GPUs)", blue)
box(ax, 6.0, 0.35, 2.0, 0.5, "one model", red_pink)
box(ax, 8.7, 0.6, 3.0, 0.35, "your metric's history  →", orange)
box(ax, 8.7, 0.1, 3.0, 0.35, "→  forecast + range", turquoise)
for x0, x1 in [(2.6, 3.3), (5.3, 6.0)]:
    ax.annotate("", xy=(x1, 0.6), xytext=(x0, 0.6), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", lw=1.5, color="grey"))
ax.annotate("", xy=(8.7, 0.6), xytext=(8.0, 0.6), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="<-", lw=1.5, color="grey"))
ax.annotate("", xy=(8.7, 0.3), xytext=(8.0, 0.5), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", lw=1.5, color="grey"))
ax.set_xlim(-0.1, 11.8)
ax.set_ylim(0, 1.05)
ax.axis("off")
plt.show()
```

- **Pretraining:** a transformer — the architecture behind ChatGPT — learns from a huge, varied pile of
  series what usually comes next.
- **Zero-shot:** you give it your history; it gives back a forecast. No fitting, no model choice.
- **Tokens:** a language model reads words; these read values or short **patches** of values. Chronos,
  for example, scales the series and turns each value into one of 4096 "words".

## Who makes them {.smaller}

| Model | From | Released | Access | Covariates | Note |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Chronos-2** | Amazon | Oct 2025 | free, runs on a laptop | yes | strong across public benchmarks |
| **TimesFM 2.5** | Google | Sep 2025 | free, runs on a laptop | yes (linear add-on) | trained mostly on Wikipedia page views |
| **TimeGPT** | Nixtla | 2023– | paid API, 30-day trial | yes | your data goes to their servers |
| **Moirai 2.0** | Salesforce | 2025 | free | yes | its first version was trained on the open LOTSA corpus |
| **TiRex** | NX-AI | 2025 | free, small (35M) | no | a recurrent (xLSTM) design |

: {tbl-colwidths="[14,11,11,22,14,28]"}

**Open** models run on your own machine — the data never leave it. **API** models need an account,
cost money at scale, and send your numbers to someone else's server: ask before you upload company data.



## Zero-shot in four lines {.smaller}

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
#| eval: false
from chronos import BaseChronosPipeline
import torch

model = BaseChronosPipeline.from_pretrained("amazon/chronos-2", device_map="cpu")   # ~500 MB, once
quantiles, mean = model.predict_quantiles([torch.tensor(history)], prediction_length=28,
                                          quantile_levels=[0.1, 0.5, 0.9])
```

That is the whole of it: no seasonal period declared, no parameters chosen, no training. These four
lines drew the P10–P90 range on the ChatGPT chart earlier.

The question is not whether it runs. It is whether it **beats "same day last week"** — on many products,
on many weeks, on data the model **cannot have seen**.

## The test: ten products, six months {.smaller}

- **Ten** daily series, from ChatGPT to Black Friday.
- **Six windows** of **28 days**, May to October 2026 — all **after** the release of every model tested,
  so none of them can have seen the answers.
- **Six** forecasters: three classical rules and models, three foundation models. The same history for
  each.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "The backtest, in code"
import timesfm
import tirex

products = ["ChatGPT", "Duolingo", "Spotify", "Netflix", "Tinder", "Strava", "TikTok", "Notion",
            "Threads", "Black Friday"]
panel = views[views["unique_id"].isin(products) & (views["ds"] >= "2023-01-01")].dropna()
H, WINDOWS = 28, 6
dates = np.sort(panel["ds"].unique())
cutoffs = [dates[len(dates) - (WINDOWS - k) * H - 1] for k in range(WINDOWS)]

tfm = timesfm.TimesFM_2p5_200M_torch.from_pretrained("google/timesfm-2.5-200m-pytorch")
tfm.compile(timesfm.ForecastConfig(max_context=1024, max_horizon=128, normalize_inputs=True,
                                   use_continuous_quantile_head=True))
tirex_model = tirex.load_model("NX-AI/TiRex", device="cpu")

frames = []
for cutoff in cutoffs:
    history = panel[panel["ds"] <= cutoff]
    window = panel[panel["ds"] > cutoff].groupby("unique_id").head(H).copy()
    classic = StatsForecast(models=[Naive(alias="Naive"), SeasonalNaive(7, alias="Seasonal naive"),
                                    AutoETS(season_length=7, alias="ETS")], freq="D")
    window = window.merge(classic.forecast(df=history[history["ds"] > cutoff - np.timedelta64(730, "D")], h=H),
                          on=["unique_id", "ds"])
    ids = sorted(history["unique_id"].unique())
    contexts = [torch.tensor(history[history["unique_id"] == i]["y"].values, dtype=torch.float32) for i in ids]
    keys = pd.DataFrame({"unique_id": np.repeat(ids, H), "ds": np.tile(np.sort(window["ds"].unique()), len(ids))})
    q, _ = chronos2.predict_quantiles(contexts, prediction_length=H, quantile_levels=[0.1, 0.5, 0.9])
    keys["Chronos-2"] = np.concatenate([np.asarray(x).reshape(-1, 3)[:, 1] for x in q])
    keys["Chronos-2 P10"] = np.concatenate([np.asarray(x).reshape(-1, 3)[:, 0] for x in q])
    keys["Chronos-2 P90"] = np.concatenate([np.asarray(x).reshape(-1, 3)[:, 2] for x in q])
    point, _ = tfm.forecast(horizon=H, inputs=[c.numpy() for c in contexts])
    keys["TimesFM"] = np.asarray(point).ravel()
    _, mean = tirex_model.forecast(context=contexts, prediction_length=H)
    keys["TiRex"] = np.asarray(mean).ravel()
    frames.append(window.merge(keys, on=["unique_id", "ds"]).assign(cutoff=cutoff))
backtest = pd.concat(frames)

scale = {}
for name in products:                                   # MAE of "same day last week", in the year before
    v = panel[(panel["unique_id"] == name) & (panel["ds"] <= cutoffs[0])]["y"].values[-365:]
    scale[name] = np.mean(np.abs(v[7:] - v[:-7]))
forecasters = ["Naive", "Seasonal naive", "ETS", "Chronos-2", "TimesFM", "TiRex"]
mase = backtest.groupby("unique_id").apply(
    lambda g: pd.Series({m: np.mean(np.abs(g["y"] - g[m])) / scale[g.name] for m in forecasters}),
    include_groups=False)
```

## The result {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="48%"}
```{python}
summary = pd.DataFrame({
    "MASE, average": mase.mean(),
    "beats seasonal naive on": mase.lt(mase["Seasonal naive"], axis=0).sum().astype(int).astype(str) + " of 10"})
summary = summary.loc[forecasters]
scoreboard(summary, rules={"MASE, average": "lower"}, size="0.9em")
```
:::

::: {.column width="52%"}
```{python}
#| label: per-product
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4.6))
order = mase["Seasonal naive"].sort_values().index
y = np.arange(len(order))
ax.scatter(mase.loc[order, "Seasonal naive"], y, color=slate, s=40, label="Seasonal naive", zorder=3)
ax.scatter(mase.loc[order, "Chronos-2"], y, color=red_pink, s=40, label="Chronos-2", zorder=3)
for i, name in enumerate(order):
    ax.plot([mase.loc[name, "Seasonal naive"], mase.loc[name, "Chronos-2"]], [i, i], color="lightgray", zorder=1)
ax.set_yticks(y, order)
ax.set_xlabel("MASE (lower is better)")
ax.legend(fontsize=8, loc="lower right")
ax.set_title("Per product: the rule vs the foundation model", fontsize=10)
plt.show()
```
:::
::::

**Chronos-2 beat "same day last week" on all ten products** with no setting chosen; TimesFM and TiRex on
nine, ETS on six. The foundation models cut the best simple rule's error by **12–16%**.

## What a 28-day forecast looks like {.smaller}

```{python}
#| label: examples
#| fig-align: center
last = backtest[backtest["cutoff"] == cutoffs[-1]]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(13, 3.4))
for ax, name in zip(axes, ["ChatGPT", "Netflix", "Spotify"]):
    hist_ = panel[(panel["unique_id"] == name) & (panel["ds"] > cutoffs[-1] - np.timedelta64(70, "D"))]
    g = last[last["unique_id"] == name]
    ax.plot(hist_["ds"], hist_["y"], color=slate, linewidth=1)
    ax.fill_between(g["ds"], g["Chronos-2 P10"], g["Chronos-2 P90"], color=red_pink, alpha=0.2)
    ax.plot(g["ds"], g["Chronos-2"], color=red_pink, linewidth=1.8, label="Chronos-2")
    ax.plot(g["ds"], g["Seasonal naive"], "--", color=blue, linewidth=1.2, label="same day last week")
    ax.set_title(f"{name}: MASE {mase.loc[name, 'Chronos-2']:.2f} vs {mase.loc[name, 'Seasonal naive']:.2f}",
                 fontsize=10)
    ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(thousands)
    ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(mdates.DateFormatter("%d %b"))
axes[0].legend(fontsize=8, loc="lower left")
plt.show()
```

The model follows each product's weekly rhythm and level; the band widens where the history has been
volatile (Netflix) and stays narrow where it has not. Spotify is the hardest series of the ten for every
method — MASE above 1 for all of them: its last months moved in a way its past did not foretell.

# Events: the part that matters most

## A predictable peak: Black Friday {.smaller}

Every year, the same week. Can a model that was never told about Black Friday see it coming from the
history alone? Forecast made on **1 October 2025**, 90 days ahead:

```{python}
#| label: black-friday
#| fig-align: center
bf = series["Black Friday"]
cut_bf = pd.Timestamp("2025-10-01")
ctx_bf = torch.tensor(bf[:cut_bf].values, dtype=torch.float32)
qb, _ = chronos2.predict_quantiles([ctx_bf], prediction_length=90, quantile_levels=[0.1, 0.5, 0.9])
qb = np.asarray(qb[0]).reshape(90, 3)
future_bf = bf[cut_bf + pd.Timedelta(days=1):][:90]
last_year = bf[cut_bf - pd.Timedelta(days=364) + pd.Timedelta(days=1):][:90].values      # same weekday, a year ago
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 3.4))
ax.plot(bf["2025-08-01":"2026-01-05"].index, bf["2025-08-01":"2026-01-05"].values, color=slate, label="actual")
ax.fill_between(future_bf.index, qb[:, 0], qb[:, 2], color=red_pink, alpha=0.2)
ax.plot(future_bf.index, qb[:, 1], color=red_pink, linewidth=1.8, label="Chronos-2, from 1 Oct")
ax.plot(future_bf.index, last_year, "--", color=blue, linewidth=1.2, label="same day last year")
ax.set_yscale("log")
ax.legend(loc="upper left", fontsize=8)
plt.show()
peak_day = future_bf.idxmax()
print(f"Actual peak {peak_day:%d %b} ({future_bf.max():,.0f} views); Chronos-2's highest day "
      f"{future_bf.index[np.argmax(qb[:, 1])]:%d %b} ({qb[:, 1].max():,.0f})")
```

It **saw the peak coming** from history alone — the right week, one day early — but **under-shot its
height** (55k against 83k). Over the 90 days it beat "same day last year" by a third (miss 1.9k vs 2.8k).

## An unpredictable peak: a campaign {.smaller}

On 11 February 2025 Duolingo announced that its mascot, the green owl, had died — a viral marketing
stunt. Page views went from about 2,000 a day to 75,000 in two days. The same model, forecasting from
the week before:

```{python}
#| label: duolingo
#| fig-align: center
duo = series["Duolingo"]
cut_d = pd.Timestamp("2025-02-04")
qd, _ = chronos2.predict_quantiles([torch.tensor(duo[:cut_d].values, dtype=torch.float32)],
                                   prediction_length=28, quantile_levels=[0.1, 0.5, 0.9])
qd = np.asarray(qd[0]).reshape(28, 3)
future_d = duo[cut_d + pd.Timedelta(days=1):][:28]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 3.2))
ax.plot(duo["2025-01-25":"2025-03-10"].index, duo["2025-01-25":"2025-03-10"].values, color=slate, label="actual")
ax.fill_between(future_d.index, qd[:, 0], qd[:, 2], color=red_pink, alpha=0.25, label="Chronos-2 P10–P90")
ax.plot(future_d.index, qd[:, 1], color=red_pink, linewidth=1.8)
ax.set_yscale("log")
ax.legend(loc="upper left", fontsize=8)
plt.show()
print(f"Peak day {future_d.idxmax():%d %b}: {future_d.max():,.0f} views; the model's P90 for that day: "
      f"{qd[np.argmax(future_d.values), 2]:,.0f}")
```

The model's **90th percentile** for the peak day: about **5,000** views; the day brought **75,000**. No
model could have known — **the marketing team did.** Such an event enters a forecast only through a
person: as a scenario, or a covariate.

## If you know the date, tell the model {.smaller}

A **covariate** is something you know about the future: a release date, a promo calendar, a holiday, a
price change. Chronos-2 can take it. Example: Lionel Messi's page views during the **2026 World Cup**,
forecast on 10 June 2026 — once from history only, once with a 0/1 "tournament day" flag.

```{python}
#| label: world-cup
#| fig-align: center
messi = views[views["unique_id"] == "Lionel Messi"][["ds", "y"]].assign(item_id="messi")
messi["y"] = np.log(messi["y"])
tournaments = [("2016-06-03", 23), ("2018-06-14", 31), ("2019-06-14", 23), ("2021-06-13", 27),
               ("2022-11-20", 28), ("2024-06-20", 24), ("2026-06-11", 38)]
messi["tournament"] = 0
for begin, days in tournaments:
    messi.loc[messi["ds"].between(begin, pd.Timestamp(begin) + pd.Timedelta(days=days)), "tournament"] = 1
before = messi[messi["ds"] < "2026-06-11"]
after = messi[messi["ds"] >= "2026-06-11"].head(51)
kw = dict(id_column="item_id", timestamp_column="ds", target="y", prediction_length=51, quantile_levels=[0.5])
alone = chronos2.predict_df(before[["item_id", "ds", "y"]], **kw)
flagged = chronos2.predict_df(before[["item_id", "ds", "y", "tournament"]],
                              future_df=after[["item_id", "ds", "tournament"]], **kw)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 3.0))
recent = messi[messi["ds"].between("2026-04-15", after["ds"].max())]
ax.plot(recent["ds"], np.exp(recent["y"]), color=slate, label="actual")
ax.plot(after["ds"], np.exp(alone["predictions"]), color=blue, linewidth=1.8, label="history only")
ax.plot(after["ds"], np.exp(flagged["predictions"]), color=red_pink, linewidth=1.8, label="+ tournament flag")
ax.axvspan(pd.Timestamp("2026-06-11"), pd.Timestamp("2026-07-19"), color=orange, alpha=0.08)
ax.set_yscale("log")
ax.legend(loc="upper left", fontsize=8)
plt.show()
y_wc = after["y"].values
print(f"Average miss (log points): history only {np.mean(np.abs(y_wc - alone['predictions'])):.2f}, "
      f"with the flag {np.mean(np.abs(y_wc - flagged['predictions'])):.2f}")
```

The flag cut the average miss by about a **third** — the model learned what a tournament does from the
six earlier ones in the history. It still under-shot the peaks. Release dates, promo calendars and
holidays are the covariates a product team always has.

## A forecast as an alarm {.smaller}

The same range makes a **monitor**: forecast each day from the days before it; if the day falls outside
the model's 1%–99% range, raise a flag. Netflix, the last 120 days:

```{python}
#| label: monitor
#| fig-align: center
nf = series["Netflix"]
days = nf.index[-120:]
ctxs = [torch.tensor(nf[:d - pd.Timedelta(days=1)].values[-1024:], dtype=torch.float32) for d in days]
qm, _ = chronos2.predict_quantiles(ctxs, prediction_length=1, quantile_levels=[0.01, 0.5, 0.99])
qm = np.stack([np.asarray(x).reshape(-1)[:3] for x in qm])
actual_m = nf[days].values
alarm = (actual_m > qm[:, 2]) | (actual_m < qm[:, 0])
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 3.2))
ax.fill_between(days, qm[:, 0], qm[:, 2], color=turquoise, alpha=0.25, label="1%–99%, forecast the day before")
ax.plot(days, actual_m, color=slate, linewidth=1, label="actual")
ax.scatter(days[alarm], actual_m[alarm], color=red_pink, s=40, zorder=3, label=f"{alarm.sum()} alarms")
ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(thousands)
ax.legend(loc="upper left", fontsize=8)
plt.show()
```

Three alarms in 120 days: few enough to read every one. The band is wide in July, after a spike, and
narrow in quiet weeks — the monitor adapts to how noisy the metric has just been, which a fixed
"±20%" rule cannot.

## Where foundation models fail {.smaller}

What the backtests and the cases say, together:

- **New events** of unknown size — a campaign, a viral moment, an outage. No model has seen *this*
  one. Plan scenarios, not a number.
- **Breaks** in the series — a tracking change, a redesigned funnel, a new market. The model extends a
  past that no longer applies. Look at the chart before you forecast it.
- **Very short histories** — a product launched last week. Better than nothing; a range wide enough to
  say so.
- **Data it may already have seen.** TimesFM was trained mostly on Wikipedia page views. Our test
  windows are after its release, so it could not have seen them — but a backtest on old public data can
  flatter any foundation model.

::: {.callout-note}
## For analysts

A test of memorisation on the M4 competition data — which is in Chronos's training corpus — found no
advantage on the windows it had seen (MATH840, week 10). Absence of evidence on one corpus is not a
guarantee on yours: prefer test periods after the model's release date.
:::

# "Can't I just ask ChatGPT?"

## The experiment {.smaller}

You can paste 56 days of numbers into a chat and ask for the next 28. We did exactly that — with a small
open language model, **Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct**, so that the experiment is free and repeatable — on the
same 10 products and 6 windows as the foundation models:

```{python}
#| echo: false
example = series["ChatGPT"][:cutoffs[-1]][-56:]
lines = [f"{day:%Y-%m-%d} ({day:%a}): {int(v)}" for day, v in example.items()]
text = ["Daily Wikipedia page views of the article 'ChatGPT':", *lines[:3], "...", lines[-1], "",
        "Forecast the next 28 days. Reply with exactly 28 integers separated by commas, nothing else."]
print("\n".join(text))
```

Sixty answers — ten products, six windows — each scored like the foundation models.

## What came back {.smaller}

```{python}
llm = pd.read_csv("../data/llm_forecasts.csv", parse_dates=["cutoff", "ds"])
llm = llm.merge(backtest[["unique_id", "ds", "y", "Seasonal naive", "Chronos-2"]], on=["unique_id", "ds"])
llm_mase = llm.groupby("unique_id").apply(
    lambda g: pd.Series({m: np.mean(np.abs(g["y"] - g[m])) / scale[g.name]
                         for m in ["LLM", "Seasonal naive", "Chronos-2"]}), include_groups=False)
answers = llm.groupby(["unique_id", "cutoff"])["numbers returned"].first()
print(f"Answers with exactly 28 numbers: {(answers == 28).sum()} of {len(answers)};  "
      f"fewer: {(answers < 28).sum()};  more: {(answers > 28).sum()}")
scoreboard(pd.DataFrame({"MASE, average": llm_mase.mean(),
                         "beats seasonal naive on": llm_mase.lt(llm_mase["Seasonal naive"], axis=0).sum()
                         .astype(int).astype(str) + " of 10"}).rename(index={"LLM": "LLM, asked in a chat"}),
           rules={"MASE, average": "lower"}, size="0.9em")
```

**Not one of 60 answers had 28 numbers** — each had to be cut or padded before it could be scored. Then
it beat "same day last week" on **3 of 10** products; Chronos-2 on 10 of 10.

## Why a chat is the wrong tool for the numbers {.smaller}

- **Numbers are text to a language model.** It writes digits one token at a time; it was trained to
  sound plausible, not to be calibrated. It can return 36 numbers when asked for 28.
- **One answer, no range.** You get a single path, not P10–P90 — and ask again, and you may get a
  different one.
- **You cannot backtest a conversation.** The honest test above needed 60 runs and a script.
- **Privacy.** Pasting company metrics into a public chat is a data decision, not a convenience.

A large chat model writes better numbers than a 1.5-billion-parameter one. None of the four points
changes.

## The right division of labour {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**The AI assistant / agent** does the work around the numbers:

- writes the data pull and the backtest script;
- runs the foundation model and the baselines;
- builds the chart and the weekly report;
- explains the result in plain language.

**The foundation model** produces the numbers and the range.

**The backtest** decides whether to trust them.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
A prompt that works:

```text
I have a CSV with columns date, value (daily
installs, 2 years). Write a Python notebook that:
1. holds out the last 4 weeks, in 6 rolling windows;
2. forecasts them with "same day last week" and with
   Chronos-2 (amazon/chronos-2), P10/P50/P90;
3. reports MASE for both and how often the actual
   value falls inside P10–P90;
4. then forecasts the next 4 weeks with the winner.
Do not tune anything on the hold-out weeks.
```
:::
::::

## A checklist for any AI-made forecast {.smaller}

Before a forecast goes into a plan, ask — or ask your agent to show:

1. **What does it beat?** "Same day last week" and "same day last year", on held-out weeks.
2. **How many windows?** One is luck. Several, in different weeks, are evidence.
3. **Is the range calibrated?** About 80% of days inside P10–P90 — counted, not assumed.
4. **What is the horizon?** Accuracy at 7 days says nothing about 90.
5. **Did the test data exist before the model was released?** If not, say so.
6. **What does it not know?** Campaigns, launches, price changes, breaks — and who adds them.
7. **What decision changes** if the truth lands at P10 instead of P50?

# Practice: a worked example, then your own

## Worked example: ChatGPT, end to end {.smaller}

One product, the whole procedure we will then repeat on your data: **look → backtest nine forecasters →
read errors, horizons and ranges → combine → forecast → conclude.**

```{python}
#| label: we-look
#| fig-align: center
we = series["ChatGPT"].asfreq("D")
recent = we[we.index >= we.index.max() - pd.Timedelta(days=3 * 365)]
rel = recent / recent.groupby(recent.index.year).transform("mean") - 1
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 3.3))
for year, g in rel.groupby(rel.index.year):
    axes[0].plot(range(7), g.groupby(g.index.dayofweek).mean().reindex(range(7)).values, "o-", label=str(year))
    axes[1].plot(range(1, 13), g.groupby(g.index.month).mean().reindex(range(1, 13)).values, "o-", label=str(year))
axes[0].set_xticks(range(7), ["Mon", "Tue", "Wed", "Thu", "Fri", "Sat", "Sun"])
axes[0].set_title("Day of week, by year (vs the year's average day)", fontsize=10)
axes[1].set_xticks(range(1, 13))
axes[1].set_title("Month, by year (vs the year's average day)", fontsize=10)
for ax in axes:
    ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(mpl.ticker.PercentFormatter(1.0))
    ax.legend(fontsize=8)
plt.show()
```

- **Week:** Tuesday–Wednesday 12–20% above the average day, Saturday 21–25% below — the same every year.
- **Year:** deep summer dips in 2024 and 2026, none in 2025 — a season, but not a stable one.
- A good forecaster reproduces the week and does not lean too hard on the year.

```{python}
#| include: false
from statsforecast.models import AutoARIMA, AutoTheta, MSTL

we_df = pd.DataFrame({"unique_id": "ChatGPT", "ds": we.index, "y": we.values})
classical_we = [Naive(alias="Naive"), SeasonalNaive(7, alias="Seasonal naive"), AutoETS(season_length=7, alias="ETS"),
                AutoARIMA(season_length=7, alias="ARIMA"), AutoTheta(season_length=7, alias="Theta"),
                MSTL(season_length=[7, 365], alias="MSTL")]
wres = StatsForecast(models=classical_we, freq="D").cross_validation(df=we_df, h=28, n_windows=6, step_size=28,
                                                                     level=[80])
parts = []
for cut in sorted(wres["cutoff"].unique()):
    ctx = torch.tensor(we[we.index <= cut].values, dtype=torch.float32)
    qc, _ = chronos2.predict_quantiles([ctx], prediction_length=28, quantile_levels=[0.1, 0.5, 0.9])
    qc = np.asarray(qc[0]).reshape(28, 3)
    pt, qt = tfm.forecast(horizon=28, inputs=[ctx.numpy()])
    qt = np.asarray(qt)[0]
    qx, mx = tirex_model.forecast(context=[ctx], prediction_length=28)
    qx = np.asarray(qx)[0]
    parts.append(pd.DataFrame({"ds": pd.date_range(cut + pd.Timedelta(days=1), periods=28), "cutoff": cut,
                               "Chronos-2": qc[:, 1], "Chronos-2-lo-80": qc[:, 0], "Chronos-2-hi-80": qc[:, 2],
                               "TimesFM": np.asarray(pt)[0], "TimesFM-lo-80": qt[:, 1], "TimesFM-hi-80": qt[:, 9],
                               "TiRex": np.asarray(mx)[0], "TiRex-lo-80": qx[:, 0], "TiRex-hi-80": qx[:, 8]}))
wres = wres.merge(pd.concat(parts), on=["ds", "cutoff"])
wres["h"] = wres.groupby("cutoff").cumcount() + 1
wres["ETS + Chronos-2"] = wres[["ETS", "Chronos-2"]].mean(axis=1)
past_we = we[we.index <= wres["cutoff"].min()].values[-365:]
scale_we = np.mean(np.abs(past_we[7:] - past_we[:-7]))
we_names = ["Naive", "Seasonal naive", "ETS", "ARIMA", "Theta", "MSTL", "Chronos-2", "TimesFM", "TiRex"]
we_board = {}
for m in we_names + ["ETS + Chronos-2"]:
    e = wres["y"] - wres[m]
    row = {"MASE": np.mean(np.abs(e)) / scale_we, "MAPE, %": 100 * np.mean(np.abs(e) / wres["y"]),
           "bias, %": 100 * np.mean(-e / wres["y"])}
    if f"{m}-lo-80" in wres:
        row["inside P10–P90"] = np.mean((wres["y"] >= wres[f"{m}-lo-80"]) & (wres["y"] <= wres[f"{m}-hi-80"]))
    we_board[m] = row
we_board = pd.DataFrame(we_board).T
```

## Nine forecasters, six windows {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{python}
scoreboard(we_board.loc[we_names], rules={"MASE": "lower", "MAPE, %": "lower", "bias, %": 0.0,
                                          "inside P10–P90": 0.8}, size="0.78em")
```
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
Six windows of 28 days, May–October 2026, as before; classical models fitted to ChatGPT alone.

- **The ranking is not the ten-product ranking.** TiRex and **Theta** — a method from 2000 — lead;
  Chronos-2, the best on the ten products, is only third.
- **MSTL** (week + year) is worst: a yearly shape that changes from year to year cannot be learned.
- **Ranges:** classical ones are too wide (almost every day inside), foundation models' too narrow
  (around 70–77%).
:::
::::

## Where the errors are {.smaller}

```{python}
#| label: we-errors
#| fig-align: center
show = ["Seasonal naive", "ETS", "Theta", "Chronos-2", "TiRex"]
by_h = wres.groupby((wres["h"] - 1) // 7).apply(
    lambda g: pd.Series({m: np.mean(np.abs(g["y"] - g[m])) / scale_we for m in show}), include_groups=False)
by_w = wres.groupby("cutoff").apply(
    lambda g: pd.Series({m: np.mean(np.abs(g["y"] - g[m])) / scale_we for m in we_names}), include_groups=False)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 3.9), width_ratios=[1, 1.4])
for m in show:
    axes[0].plot(by_h.index + 1, by_h[m], "o-", label=m)
axes[0].set_xticks(by_h.index + 1)
axes[0].set_xlabel("week of the horizon")
axes[0].set_ylabel("MASE")
axes[0].legend(fontsize=8)
im = axes[1].imshow(by_w.T.values, cmap="RdYlGn_r", vmin=0.2, vmax=1.6, aspect="auto")
axes[1].set_yticks(range(len(we_names)), we_names)
axes[1].set_xticks(range(len(by_w)), [f"{c:%d %b}" for c in by_w.index])
for i in range(len(we_names)):
    for j in range(len(by_w)):
        axes[1].text(j, i, f"{by_w.iloc[j, i]:.2f}", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=7)
axes[1].set_title("MASE by backtest window (last day of history)", fontsize=10)
plt.show()
```

- **The first week is the easy one** — about half the error of weeks 2–4. Re-forecast weekly.
- **Windows differ more than models.** The May window is hard for everyone, August easy for most; MSTL
  falls apart in June (3.6). Any single window would have told a different story.

## Ranges and a combination {.smaller}

```{python}
#| label: we-coverage
#| fig-align: center
covered = we_board["inside P10–P90"].dropna()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 2.2))
ax.bar(covered.index, covered.values,
       color=[red_pink if m in ("Chronos-2", "TimesFM", "TiRex") else slate for m in covered.index])
ax.axhline(0.8, color="black", linewidth=1, linestyle="--")
ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(mpl.ticker.PercentFormatter(1.0))
ax.set_ylim(0, 1.05)
ax.set_title("Share of days inside the 80% range — the dashed line is the target", fontsize=10)
plt.show()
```

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
```{python}
scoreboard(we_board.loc[["ETS", "Chronos-2", "ETS + Chronos-2"], ["MASE", "MAPE, %"]], size="0.85em")
```
:::

::: {.column width="55%"}
- A range is a promise; **count** how often it is kept, and widen or narrow it by what you see.
- The **average of ETS and Chronos-2** — a pair fixed *before* looking at scores — beats both of its
  parts. Picking the single winner by its test score is the mistake a backtest exists to prevent.
:::
::::

## The next four weeks {.smaller}

```{python}
#| label: we-final
#| fig-align: center
mid, lo, hi = (lambda q: (q[:, 1], q[:, 0], q[:, 2]))(np.asarray(
    chronos2.predict_quantiles([torch.tensor(we.values, dtype=torch.float32)], prediction_length=28,
                               quantile_levels=[0.1, 0.5, 0.9])[0][0]).reshape(28, 3))
ets_final = StatsForecast(models=[AutoETS(season_length=7)], freq="D").forecast(df=we_df, h=28)["AutoETS"].values
future_we = pd.date_range(we.index[-1] + pd.Timedelta(days=1), periods=28)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 3.3))
ax.plot(we.index[-90:], we.values[-90:], color=slate, linewidth=1, label="actual")
ax.fill_between(future_we, lo, hi, color=red_pink, alpha=0.2, label="Chronos-2 P10–P90")
ax.plot(future_we, mid, color=red_pink, linewidth=2, label="Chronos-2")
ax.plot(future_we, (mid + ets_final) / 2, "--", color=blue, linewidth=1.5, label="ETS + Chronos-2")
ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(thousands)
ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(mdates.DateFormatter("%d %b"))
ax.legend(loc="upper left", fontsize=8)
plt.show()
print(f"Highest P90 day: {future_we[np.argmax(hi)]:%a %d %b}, {hi.max() / 1000:.0f}k views;  "
      f"lowest P10 day: {future_we[np.argmin(lo)]:%a %d %b}, {lo.min() / 1000:.0f}k")
```

Read it as a plan: weekdays up to the P90 line for capacity, weekends for maintenance. The series jumped
in its last week; the forecast falls back towards the usual pattern, and the width of the range is how
unsure it is that the jump will fade.

## What the worked example says {.smaller}

1. **Backtest on your own series.** The best model on ten products is third on this one; a 2000-era
   method is near the top. No ranking transfers.
2. **Baselines first.** Six of eight models beat "same day last week" — by margins, not miracles; two did
   not beat it at all.
3. **Mind the horizon.** Week one is about twice as accurate as the weeks after it: re-forecast weekly.
4. **Check the range before you use it.** Too wide for the classical models, too narrow for the
   foundation models — here. Count it on your data.
5. **Combine.** A classical and a foundation model, averaged by a rule fixed in advance, beat both.

The full analysis, with every chart and table, is a notebook you can read without running:
**[worked example (Colab)](https://colab.research.google.com/github/Aranaur/aranaur.rbind.io/blob/main/lectures/genesis/sdb/labs/worked_example.ipynb)**.

## Your turn: the template {.smaller}

**[→ Open the template in Google Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/github/Aranaur/aranaur.rbind.io/blob/main/lectures/genesis/sdb/labs/template.ipynb)**
— the same toolkit, for your series. Change one cell, run everything.

1. **Settings:** a product from today's ten, or your own CSV (date, value — daily or weekly; public or
   anonymised data only); the season, the horizon, the number of windows; which forecasters to compare.
2. **Run:** the notebook draws your data, backtests, scores, and forecasts with the backtest winner.
3. **Conclude:** four questions at the end — who won and by how much, is the range calibrated, how fast
   does the error grow, and what does the forecast not know?

In teams: bring one result each, and compare where the foundation models won — and where a 2000-era
method did not lose.

## What to take away {.smaller}

- A forecast is a **number, a range, a horizon and a decision** — the range matters as much as the
  number.
- **Baselines first, backtests always.** "Same day last week" is the bar; one lucky window is not
  evidence.
- **Foundation models** are a real step: free, fast, no tuning — and on our ten products they beat the
  classical rules on almost every one.
- They **do not know your calendar.** Predictable seasons they learn from history; campaigns, launches
  and breaks you must tell them — or plan scenarios around.
- **Language models are for the work around the numbers**, not for the numbers. Let the agent write the
  backtest, let the foundation model forecast, let the backtest decide.
